questions.q: What does `git blame <file>` actually show you?
options: Which lines currently have syntax errors
A list of every branch that has touched the file
Which commit, author, and date last changed each line of the file
The total number of bugs in the file
questions.explain: git blame annotates each line with the commit, author, and timestamp that most recently modified it.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why is "blame" a somewhat misleading name for the command?
options: Because it only works on deleted files
Because it actually deletes the blamed commit
Because its real use is finding the fastest path to the reasoning behind a line, not assigning fault
Because it requires administrator access
questions.explain: The lesson frames git blame as a way to trace a line back to the commit message, PR, or ticket that explains why it's written that way — not a fault-finder.

questions.q: After git blame gives you a commit hash, what's the typical next step to understand the full reasoning?
options: Immediately delete that commit
Run git show on that hash to read the full commit message and diff
Run git clone again
There is no next step — the hash alone explains everything
questions.explain: git show displays the full commit message and diff for a specific commit, which is where the actual explanation for a change usually lives.

questions.q: What makes `git log -S "SOME_STRING"` (the pickaxe) different from `git blame` on a current file?
options: It only searches commit messages, never diffs
It searches every commit's diff for the string, including commits that removed it entirely — something blame on the current file can't show
It is a faster but otherwise identical version of git blame
It only works on the main branch
questions.explain: Because git blame only annotates lines that currently exist in the file, it can't show you a commit that deleted code; the pickaxe searches the full diff history instead.

Pushes the file to a remote repository

questions.explain: The -p flag shows the actual diff (patch) for each commit touching the file, letting you read its full change history in order.
